claim: Cellulose and hemicellulose are the two major polysaccharides found in the plant cell wall.
source: In current industrial methods, cellulose and hemicellulose, the two major polysaccharides found in the plant cell wall (Somerville et al., 2004), are generally processed into monomers of glucose and xylose, respectively (Chundawat et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Somerville et al., 2004, which provides external scholarly support for this statement.

claim: Cellulose and hemicellulose are generally processed into monomers of glucose and xylose, respectively.
source: In current industrial methods, cellulose and hemicellulose, the two major polysaccharides found in the plant cell wall (Somerville et al., 2004), are generally processed into monomers of glucose and xylose, respectively (Chundawat et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chundawat et al., 2011, indicating established knowledge in the field.

claim: Large quantities of cellulase and hemicellulase enzyme cocktails are required to release monosaccharides from plant cell wall polymers.
source: In addition to harsh pretreatment of biomass, large quantities of cellulase and hemicellulase enzyme cocktails are required to release monosaccharides from plant cell wall polymers, posing unsolved economic and logistical challenges (Lynd et al., 2002; Himmel et al., 2007; Jarboe et al., 2010; Chundawat et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Lynd et al., 2002; Himmel et al., 2007; Jarboe et al., 2010; Chundawat et al., 2011) indicating established knowledge.

claim: S. cerevisiae requires substantial engineering to ferment sugars derived from plant cell walls such as cellobiose and xylose.
source: The bioethanol industry currently uses the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae to ferment sugars derived from cornstarch or sugarcane into ethanol (Hong and Nielsen, 2012), but S. cerevisiae requires substantial engineering to ferment sugars derived from plant cell walls such as cellobiose and xylose (Kuyper et al., 2005; Jeffries, 2006; van Maris et al., 2007; Ha et al., 2011; Hong and Nielsen, 2012; Young et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Kuyper et al., 2005; Jeffries, 2006; van Maris et al., 2007; Ha et al., 2011; Hong and Nielsen, 2012; Young et al., 2014).

claim: Neurospora crassa naturally grows well on the cellulose and hemicellulose components of the plant cell wall.
source: In contrast to S. cerevisiae, many cellulolytic fungi including Neurospora crassa (Tian et al., 2009) naturally grow well on the cellulose and hemicellulose components of the plant cell wall.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tian et al., 2009.

claim: A strain of N. crassa carrying a deletion of CDT-2 was unable to grow on xylan.
source: A strain carrying a deletion of a previously identified cellodextrin transporter (CDT-2, NCU08114) (Galazka et al., 2010) was unable to grow on xylan (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and xylodextrins remained in the culture supernatant (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Xylodextrins remained in the culture supernatant of N. crassa strain with CDT-2 deletion.
source: A strain carrying a deletion of a previously identified cellodextrin transporter (CDT-2, NCU08114) (Galazka et al., 2010) was unable to grow on xylan (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and xylodextrins remained in the culture supernatant (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: S. cerevisiae strains expressing cdt-2 were able to import xylobiose, xylotriose, and xylotetraose.
source: As a direct test of transport function of CDT-2, S. cerevisiae strains expressing cdt-2 were able to import xylobiose, xylotriose, and xylotetraose (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: N. crassa expresses a putative intracellular β-xylosidase, GH43-2 (NCU01900), when grown on xylan.
source: Notably, N. crassa expresses a putative intracellular β-xylosidase, GH43-2 (NCU01900), when grown on xylan (Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2012.

claim: Purified GH43-2 displayed robust hydrolase activity towards xylodextrins with a degree of polymerization spanning from 2 to 8.
source: Purified GH43-2 displayed robust hydrolase activity towards xylodextrins with a degree of polymerization (DP) spanning from 2 to 8, and with a pH optimum near 7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: GH43-2 has a pH optimum near 7.
source: Purified GH43-2 displayed robust hydrolase activity towards xylodextrins with a degree of polymerization (DP) spanning from 2 to 8, and with a pH optimum near 7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Orthologues of cdt-2 are widely distributed in the fungal kingdom.
source: As with cdt-1, orthologues of cdt-2 are widely distributed in the fungal kingdom (Galazka et al., 2010), suggesting that many fungi consume xylodextrins derived from plant cell walls.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Galazka et al., 2010.

claim: Many fungi consume xylodextrins derived from plant cell walls.
source: As with cdt-1, orthologues of cdt-2 are widely distributed in the fungal kingdom (Galazka et al., 2010), suggesting that many fungi consume xylodextrins derived from plant cell walls.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the wide distribution of cdt-2 orthologues.

claim: Intracellular β-xylosidases are widespread in fungi.
source: Furthermore, as with intracellular β-glucosidases (Galazka et al., 2010), intracellular β-xylosidases are also widespread in fungi (Sun et al., 2012) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2012 and phylogenetic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Cellodextrins and xylodextrins derived from plant cell walls are not catabolized by wild-type S. cerevisiae.
source: Cellodextrins and xylodextrins derived from plant cell walls are not catabolized by wild-type S. cerevisiae (Matsushika et al., 2009; Galazka et al., 2010; Young et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Matsushika et al., 2009; Galazka et al., 2010; Young et al., 2010).

claim: Reconstitution of a cellodextrin transport and consumption pathway from N. crassa in S. cerevisiae enabled this yeast to ferment cellobiose.
source: Reconstitution of a cellodextrin transport and consumption pathway from N. crassa in S. cerevisiae enabled this yeast to ferment cellobiose (Galazka et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Galazka et al., 2010.

claim: S. cerevisiae was engineered to consume xylose by introducing xylose isomerase (XI), or by introducing xylose reductase (XR) and xylitol dehydrogenase (XDH).
source: Previously, S. cerevisiae was engineered to consume xylose by introducing xylose isomerase (XI), or by introducing xylose reductase (XR) and xylitol dehydrogenase (XDH) (Jeffries, 2006; van Maris et al., 2007; Matsushika et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Jeffries, 2006; van Maris et al., 2007; Matsushika et al., 2009).

claim: The xylose utilizing yeast expressing CDT-2 along with the intracellular β-xylosidase GH43-2 was able to directly utilize xylodextrins with DPs of 2 or 3.
source: The xylose utilizing yeast expressing CDT-2 along with the intracellular β-xylosidase GH43-2 was able to directly utilize xylodextrins with DPs of 2 or 3 (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: High cell density cultures of the engineered yeast were capable of consuming xylodextrins with DPs up to 5.
source: Notably, although high cell density cultures of the engineered yeast were capable of consuming xylodextrins with DPs up to 5, xylose levels remained high (Figure 1C), suggesting the existence of severe bottlenecks in the engineered yeast.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Xylose levels remained high in high cell density cultures of the engineered yeast consuming xylodextrins.
source: Notably, although high cell density cultures of the engineered yeast were capable of consuming xylodextrins with DPs up to 5, xylose levels remained high (Figure 1C), suggesting the existence of severe bottlenecks in the engineered yeast.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Xylodextrins were converted into xylosyl-xylitol oligomers in yeast strains expressing CDT-2, GH43-2 and the S. stipitis XR/XDH pathway.
source: Analyses of the supernatants from cultures of the yeast strains expressing CDT-2, GH43-2 and the S. stipitis XR/XDH pathway surprisingly revealed that the xylodextrins were converted into xylosyl-xylitol oligomers, a set of previously unknown compounds rather than hydrolyzed to xylose and consumed (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Xylosyl-xylitol oligomers are previously unknown compounds.
source: Analyses of the supernatants from cultures of the yeast strains expressing CDT-2, GH43-2 and the S. stipitis XR/XDH pathway surprisingly revealed that the xylodextrins were converted into xylosyl-xylitol oligomers, a set of previously unknown compounds rather than hydrolyzed to xylose and consumed (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is stated explicitly in the text as a novel finding.

claim: The resulting xylosyl-xylitol oligomers were effectively dead-end products that could not be metabolized further.
source: The resulting xylosyl-xylitol oligomers were effectively dead-end products that could not be metabolized further.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that these compounds accumulated and were not consumed.

claim: Xylobiose can fit well in the active site pocket of CtXR according to computational docking.
source: Using computational docking algorithms (Trott and Olson, 2010), xylobiose was found to fit well in the pocket.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 2B and cited methodology.

claim: There are no obstructions in the CtXR protein that would prevent longer xylodextrin oligomers from binding.
source: Furthermore, there are no obstructions in the protein that would prevent longer xylodextrin oligomers from binding (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: N. crassa xylose reductase XYR-1 (NCU08384) generated xylosyl-xylitol products from xylodextrins.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, xylose reductase XYR-1 (NCU08384) from N. crassa also generated xylosyl-xylitol products from xylodextrins (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No xylosyl-xylitol byproduct accumulated in the culture medium when N. crassa was grown on xylan.
source: However, when N. crassa was grown on xylan, no xylosyl-xylitol byproduct accumulated in the culture medium (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: GH43-7 (NCU09625) is a second putative intracellular β-xylosidase upregulated when N. crassa was grown on xylan.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, a second putative intracellular β-xylosidase upregulated when N. crassa was grown on xylan, GH43-7 (NCU09625) (Sun et al., 2012), had weak β-xylosidase activity but rapidly hydrolyzed xylosyl-xylitol into xylose and xylitol (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2012.

claim: GH43-7 had weak β-xylosidase activity but rapidly hydrolyzed xylosyl-xylitol into xylose and xylitol.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, a second putative intracellular β-xylosidase upregulated when N. crassa was grown on xylan, GH43-7 (NCU09625) (Sun et al., 2012), had weak β-xylosidase activity but rapidly hydrolyzed xylosyl-xylitol into xylose and xylitol (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: GH43-7 is widely distributed in fungi and bacteria.
source: The newly identified xylosyl-xylitol-specific β-xylosidase GH43-7 is widely distributed in fungi and bacteria (Figure 2E), suggesting that it is used by a variety of microbes in the consumption of xylodextrins.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: GH43-7 enzymes from Bacillus subtilis and Escherichia coli cleave both xylodextrin and xylosyl-xylitol.
source: Indeed, GH43-7 enzymes from the bacteria Bacillus subtilis and Escherichia coli cleave both xylodextrin and xylosyl-xylitol (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: N. crassa, T. reesei, A. nidulans and B. subtilis all produce xylosyl-xylitols when grown on xylodextrins.
source: Notably, these widely divergent fungi and B. subtilis all produce xylosyl-xylitols when grown on xylodextrins (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The organisms that produce xylosyl-xylitols span over 1 billion years of evolution.
source: These organisms span over 1 billion years of evolution (Figure 3B), indicating that the use of xylodextrin reductases to consume plant hemicellulose is widespread.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic data shown in Figure 3B and citations (Wellman et al. (2003); Galagan et al. (2005); Hedges et al. (2006)).

claim: The use of xylodextrin reductases to consume plant hemicellulose is widespread.
source: These organisms span over 1 billion years of evolution (Figure 3B), indicating that the use of xylodextrin reductases to consume plant hemicellulose is widespread.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the evolutionary distribution of organisms producing xylosyl-xylitols.

claim: GH43-7 enabled S. cerevisiae to grow more rapidly on xylodextrin when combined with CDT-2 and GH43-2.
source: When combined with the original xylodextrin pathway (CDT-2 plus GH43-2), GH43-7 enabled S. cerevisiae to grow more rapidly on xylodextrin (Figure 4A) and eliminated accumulation of xylosyl-xylitol intermediates (Figure 4B–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GH43-7 eliminated accumulation of xylosyl-xylitol intermediates when combined with CDT-2 and GH43-2.
source: When combined with the original xylodextrin pathway (CDT-2 plus GH43-2), GH43-7 enabled S. cerevisiae to grow more rapidly on xylodextrin (Figure 4A) and eliminated accumulation of xylosyl-xylitol intermediates (Figure 4B–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of xylose and glucose greatly improved anaerobic fermentation of xylodextrins.
source: The presence of xylose and glucose greatly improved anaerobic fermentation of xylodextrins (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating that metabolic sensing in S. cerevisiae with the complete xylodextrin pathway may require additional tuning (Youk and van Oudenaarden, 2009) for optimal xylodextrin fermentation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: The XR/XDH pathway produced much less xylitol when xylodextrins were used in fermentations than from xylose.
source: Notably, we observed that the XR/XDH pathway produced much less xylitol when xylodextrins were used in fermentations than from xylose (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The XR/XDH pathway widely used in engineered S. cerevisiae naturally has broad substrate specificity for xylodextrins.
source: Taken together, these results reveal that the XR/XDH pathway widely used in engineered S. cerevisiae naturally has broad substrate specificity for xylodextrins, and complete reconstitution of the naturally occurring xylodextrin pathway is necessary to enable S. cerevisiae to efficiently consume xylodextrins.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing XR can reduce xylodextrins.

claim: Complete reconstitution of the naturally occurring xylodextrin pathway is necessary to enable S. cerevisiae to efficiently consume xylodextrins.
source: Taken together, these results reveal that the XR/XDH pathway widely used in engineered S. cerevisiae naturally has broad substrate specificity for xylodextrins, and complete reconstitution of the naturally occurring xylodextrin pathway is necessary to enable S. cerevisiae to efficiently consume xylodextrins.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that all three components (CDT-2, GH43-2, GH43-7) are needed for efficient xylodextrin consumption.

claim: Simultaneous fermentation of sucrose and xylodextrins was observed with increased ethanol yields.
source: We observe simultaneous fermentation of sucrose and xylodextrins, with increased ethanol yields (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The levels of xylitol production were found to be low in cofermentations with glucose.
source: Notably, the levels of xylitol production were found to be low (Figure 6), as observed in cofermentations with glucose (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 5B.

claim: In bacteria such as B. subtilis, xylosyl-xylitol may be generated by aldo-keto reductases known to possess broad substrate specificity.
source: In bacteria such as B. subtilis, xylosyl-xylitol may be generated by aldo-keto reductases known to possess broad substrate specificity (Barski et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by a citation to Barski et al., 2008 about aldo-keto reductases.

claim: The breakdown of hemicellulose releases highly toxic acetate.
source: The breakdown of hemicellulose, which is acetylated (Sun et al., 2012), releases highly toxic acetate, degrading the performance of S. cerevisiae fermentations (Bellissimi et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bellissimi et al., 2009 and Sun et al., 2012.

claim: The cofactor imbalance problem of the XR/XDH pathway can be exploited to drive acetate reduction, thereby detoxifying the fermentation medium and increasing ethanol production.
source: The cofactor imbalance problem of the XR/XDH pathway, which can lead to accumulation of reduced byproducts (xylitol and glycerol) and therefore was deemed a problem, can be exploited to drive acetate reduction, thereby detoxifying the fermentation medium and increasing ethanol production (Wei et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wei et al., 2013.

claim: Xylodextrins released from sugarcane bagasse by compressed hot water treatment could be directly fermented by yeast engineered to consume xylodextrins.
source: For example, we propose that xylodextrins released from the hemicellulose in sugarcane bagasse by using compressed hot water treatment (Hendriks and Zeeman, 2009; Agbor et al., 2011; Vallejos et al., 2012) could be directly fermented by yeast engineered to consume xylodextrins, as we have shown in proof-of-principle experiments (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is speculative but supported by proof-of-principle experimental data shown in Figure 6 and citations.

claim: Xylodextrin consumption combined with glucose or cellodextrin consumption could improve next-generation biofuel production from lignocellulosic feedstocks.
source: Xylodextrin consumption combined with glucose or cellodextrin consumption (Figure 7) could also improve next-generation biofuel production from lignocellulosic feedstocks under a number of pretreatment scenarios (Hendriks and Zeeman, 2009; Vallejos et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citations to Hendriks and Zeeman, 2009 and Vallejos et al., 2012.

claim: CDT-2 is a cellodextrin transporter previously identified.
source: A strain carrying a deletion of a previously identified cellodextrin transporter (CDT-2, NCU08114) (Galazka et al., 2010) was unable to grow on xylan (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and xylodextrins remained in the culture supernatant (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Galazka et al., 2010.

claim: The results with CDT-2 and GH43-2 confirm those obtained independently in Cai et al. (2014).
source: The results with CDT-2 and GH43-2 confirm those obtained independently in Cai et al. (2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cai et al. (2014).

claim: Endogenous yeast enzymes and GH43-2 transglycolysis activity are not responsible for generating the xylosyl-xylitol byproducts.
source: These results indicate that endogenous yeast enzymes and GH43-2 transglycolysis activity are not responsible for generating the xylosyl-xylitol byproducts, that is, that they must be generated by the XR from S. stipitis (SsXR).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the co-culture experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Xylosyl-xylitol byproducts must be generated by the XR from S. stipitis (SsXR).
source: These results indicate that endogenous yeast enzymes and GH43-2 transglycolysis activity are not responsible for generating the xylosyl-xylitol byproducts, that is, that they must be generated by the XR from S. stipitis (SsXR).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the co-culture experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CtXR contains an open active site cavity where xylose could bind, located near the binding site for the NADH co-factor.
source: CtXR contains an open active site cavity where xylose could bind, located near the binding site for the NADH co-factor (Kavanagh et al., 2002; Kratzer et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kavanagh et al., 2002 and Kratzer et al., 2006.

claim: The open shape of the CtXR active site can readily accommodate the binding of longer xylodextrin substrates.
source: Notably, the open shape of the active site can readily accommodate the binding of longer xylodextrin substrates (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: N. crassa presumably expresses an additional enzymatic activity to consume xylosyl-xylitol oligomers.
source: Thus, N. crassa presumably expresses an additional enzymatic activity to consume xylosyl-xylitol oligomers.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that xylosyl-xylitol does not accumulate in N. crassa cultures.

claim: Metabolic sensing in S. cerevisiae with the complete xylodextrin pathway may require additional tuning for optimal xylodextrin fermentation.
source: The presence of xylose and glucose greatly improved anaerobic fermentation of xylodextrins (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), indicating that metabolic sensing in S. cerevisiae with the complete xylodextrin pathway may require additional tuning (Youk and van Oudenaarden, 2009) for optimal xylodextrin fermentation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations and supported by a citation to Youk and van Oudenaarden, 2009.

claim: The 6-methoxy group distinguishes glucose derivatives from xylose.
source: The 6-methoxy group (blue) distinguishes glucose derivatives from xylose.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in Figure 1A caption.

claim: GH43-7 is used by a variety of microbes in the consumption of xylodextrins.
source: The newly identified xylosyl-xylitol-specific β-xylosidase GH43-7 is widely distributed in fungi and bacteria (Figure 2E), suggesting that it is used by a variety of microbes in the consumption of xylodextrins.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the wide distribution of GH43-7 shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Intracellular cellobiose utilization requires CDT-1 or CDT-2 along with β-glucosidase GH1-1.
source: Intracellular cellobiose utilization requires CDT-1 or CDT-2 along with β-glucosidase GH1-1 (Galazka et al., 2010) and enters glycolysis after phosphorylation by hexokinases (HXK) to form glucose-6-phosphate (Glc-6-P).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Galazka et al., 2010 and shown in Figure 7.

claim: Intracellular xylodextrin utilization uses CDT-2 and requires the intracellular β-xylosidases GH43-2 and GH43-7.
source: Intracellular xylodextrin utilization also uses CDT-2 and requires the intracellular β-xylosidases GH43-2 and GH43-7.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript and summarized in Figure 7.

claim: The resulting xylose from xylodextrin breakdown can be assimilated through the pentose phosphate pathway consisting of xylose/xylodextrin reductase (XR), xylitol dehydrogenase (XDH), and xylulokinase (XK).
source: The resulting xylose can be assimilated through the pentose phosphate pathway consisting of xylose/xylodextrin reductase (XR), xylitol dehydrogenase (XDH), and xylulokinase (XK).
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge of xylose metabolism and shown in Figure 7.
